articles.title: Catastrophic GTA VI leak is a full working build — notorious hacker CyberLeek taunts Rockstar Games by spraying the word 'leek' onto a wall in-game with bullets
articles.text:
Catastrophic GTA VI leak is a full working build — notorious hacker CyberLeek taunts Rockstar Games by spraying the word 'leek' onto a wall in-game with bullets
It's unclear how Cyberleek got their hands on the game.
Hacker Cyberleek, who’s protesting Rockstar’s pre-selling of digital copies of GTA VI by releasing gameplay clips and the entire map of Leonidas, has once again released video clips on their website. Per videos online, the leaker apparently has a complete, unreleased game build, with the clip showing in-game footage of the character spelling out the LEEK by shooting at a wall, revealing that they have recorded themselves playing the game, rather than simply accessing internal recordings or video.
Rockstar has been quick to combat these leaks by issuing DMCA takedown notices, especially on YouTube, but it seems that some clips are still available on X. Aside from that, the leaker’s website is still active, although it seems that its server gets overwhelmed sometimes, returning a 502 Bad Gateway response. This could potentially be disastrous for the company, especially as the hacker threatened to keep on releasing leaks until the GTA VI maker issues a public apology with “a concrete commitment to be better.” Kuba even said that Cyberleek could potentially release the ending of the game, spoiling it for everyone.
It’s unclear how Cyberleek got their hands on such a complete GTA VI build, especially as it isn’t pegged to launch until November. More than that, the game will also be released on console first, with no announcement date yet for when the PC version will arrive. But because GTA VI is such a highly anticipated game, with some fans going to great lengths to predict when its next trailer will come out, it’s also a juicy target for some bad actors. In fact, the company was hit by a hack back in April, with the group threatening to release confidential data if the company did not pay up.
The previous leaks were supposedly based on footage that’s already a year old, but many members of the community agree that the recent leaks are new ones. As many are saying that the most recent leaks are from the game build, Rockstar has its work cut out, with the company issuing takedown notices left and right. The company could actually just release the extended look early, taking the flame out of these leaks, but it likely couldn’t do that because of its deal with Netflix, which will show the third trailer starting August 27. Still, we don’t know how much damage Cyberleek is going to do to the game, especially as many people will still likely purchase it despite the leaks. Nevertheless, the people who worked on GTA VI would probably be displeased to see their work leaked out on the internet.

articles.title: Zero Networks expands Palo Alto Networks integration to AI agent control - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Zero Networks expands Palo Alto Networks integration to AI agent control
Zero-trust security startup Zero Networks Ltd. today expanded its integration with Palo Alto Networks Inc., adding automated threat containment and a set of controls aimed at artificial intelligence agents.
The two companies first integrated their products in February 2025. Zero Networks discovers and tags assets without agents. Palo Alto Networks firewalls take that context in as Dynamic Address Groups, and the policy follows a device when it moves.
The expansion pushes the pairing from policy orchestration into enforcement. Customers can now contain a compromised asset on its own instead of pulling an entire segment offline. Selected traffic from protected workloads can also be routed to Palo Alto Networks firewalls for Layer 7 threat prevention, which puts deep inspection on internal east-west traffic that would usually stay inside the segment it started in. Anything flagged as malicious gets blocked and the affected asset is cut off.
Redirection runs on Linux systems today. Windows support is planned, which would extend the same inspection and containment to the Windows systems that make up much of the enterprise attack surface.
Assets and policies managed by Zero Networks now surface inside Strata Cloud Manager, the Palo Alto Networks management console. Security teams see what has been discovered, which segmentation policies apply and which firewall controls are inspecting the traffic, all in one place. Dynamic tagging keeps that view accurate as workloads shift and IP addresses change, in place of hand-maintained static rules.
The second half of the announcement ties Zero Networks AI Segmentation, launched in April, to Prisma AIRS, the Palo Alto Networks product for securing AI traffic. AI agents connect straight into applications, models, databases and production systems, normally carrying valid credentials and broad permissions.
Zero Networks said that makes manipulated or compromised activity hard to tell apart from ordinary automation. Its software identifies the agents and fixes deterministic, identity-based boundaries around where each one is allowed to connect. Unsanctioned AI services can be blocked outright. Where a closer look is warranted, the traffic goes to Prisma AIRS for inspection of the prompts, responses and data moving through the interaction.
Co-founder and Chief Executive Benny Lakunishok said customers “should not have to stitch together separate controls” for their firewalls, internal assets and AI agents. The expanded integration gives them a single enforcement model, he said, with Zero Networks deciding which connections are permitted and Palo Alto Networks running the deep inspection.
Neither company is asking customers to redesign the network for any of this. The joint solution runs on enforcement capabilities both platforms already ship, across on-premises, cloud, operational technology, Kubernetes and hybrid environments.
Automated microsegmentation, dynamic asset tagging, policy synchronization and Linux traffic redirection are available now. The Prisma AIRS integration and Windows traffic redirection has not been given a release date.
Zero Networks was founded in 2019 and has raised more than $100 million in funding. Highland Europe Ltd. led its $55 million Series C in June 2025.

articles.title: As demand for Meta AI glasses explodes, it’s harder to avoid creepy recordings
articles.text:
Can you tell when someone nearby is wearing Meta AI glasses?
As millions of people buy into the smart glasses fad each year, the odds are increasing that you could be secretly recorded while simply going about your day.
Meta is not the only smart glasses maker, but its AI glasses are by far the most popular. And as the devices become more common, some public places, including schools, courts, restaurants, and entertainment venues, have begun to ban them. Even tech lovers have rejected Meta glasses in certain settings. The hackers behind DEF CON 2026 reportedly banned smart glasses with no exceptions, reminding attendees with prescription pairs to “be sure to pack non-violating eyewear if you need them.”
But a ban is only as effective as the people enforcing it. Spotting a pair of smart glasses can require tech-savvy security staff, and enforcement may depend on users voluntarily disclosing their devices—or on watchful observers speaking up.
Those bans are an important way to push back against the potential for abuse. But privacy advocates know that increasing the social friction around nonconsensual recording can’t stop the practice by itself.
Until comprehensive consumer privacy laws are passed, the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) has warned that Meta seems prepared to make the tech even more invasive in its bid to sell more glasses and stay ahead of rivals in the burgeoning industry.
And as AI advances, EFF staff technologist Cooper Quintin told Ars, potential new features such as facial recognition could raise the stakes further, potentially allowing the devices to be used to create convincing deepfakes or nonconsensual intimate imagery of people who may not be aware that cameras are rolling.
“I think that there are a lot of other concerns there beyond just being recorded without your knowledge,” Quintin told Ars.
EFF has warned that smart glasses makers will likely be tempted to add facial-recognition features unless lawmakers intervene and give people a private right to sue companies whose products violate their biometric privacy rights. In the meantime, the group has released a guide for smart-glasses users that lays out ways to resist facial recognition, develop responsible recording habits, and better understand the privacy risks of continuous recording. It also urges users to consider blurring strangers’ faces before posting videos online.
For people unknowingly targeted in secret recordings, the only safety feature Meta provides is nearly “useless,” Quintin told Ars.
A tiny recording light that can be easily covered with a sticker is unlikely to deter bad actors intent on abusing the glasses, whether stalkers or creepy partners secretly recording women in public bathrooms or private bedrooms. The tech has also controversially been used in immigration raids, 404 Media reported, and to harass sex workers and retail workers. And on social media, videos show a range of other unwanted recordings, from relatively inoffensive pranks to more harmful videos featuring bullying or harassment.
The volume of these videos online suggests the LED feature “is better than nothing, but not by much,” Quintin said.
Hobbyists build apps to detect glasses
Experts have noted that Meta may already have plans to diminish that limited safety feature. The company is supposedly “testing a prototype of ‘super sensing’ AI glasses that would use cameras and audio recordings to capture a wearer’s every moment,” the Financial Times reported last month. According to sources familiar with Meta’s thinking, executives “are planning not to activate the LED when the super-sensing features are being used,” even though “that would make it harder for bystanders to know when they were being recorded.”
Meta execs’ plans may change if the public’s privacy concerns remain a sticking point, though, sources have suggested. And backlash will likely be sustained as more people wear the glasses, since digital rights experts have accused Meta of failing to consider civil rights or privacy ramifications when designing new features. Perhaps most troublingly, Meta recently backpedaled and deleted an unreleased facial recognition system from its smart-glasses app that Wired and EFF revealed had been quietly installed on 50 million phones in June.
It’s unclear if or when Meta might try to bring the facial recognition system back. Meta did not respond to Ars’ request to comment on this story.
As Meta glasses have become more commonplace, hobbyist programmers have been building apps to detect when smart glasses are nearby so people can steer clear of them.
These civil defense apps, Quintin said, aren’t a perfect solution to the social problem of smart-glasses recording without consent. But when used in combination with bans, the apps can offer wary members of the public a way to check if a ban is being enforced or whether a nearby device may begin recording at a sensitive time. Society needs both solutions, Quintin said, especially because the most popular and recognizable smart glasses available today will likely one day come in a wider assortment of trendy models, making them harder to spot in the wild.
“You need to have the social construct around these being unwelcome, and you also need to be able to find when people are using these,” Quintin said. “Right now, they’re pretty easy to just detect with your eyes. They’re pretty obvious, but that might not always be the case. So technologies like this are also important to supplement that.”
“I can do something about it”
Since February, engineers have been releasing and updating apps that help people detect glasses like Ray-Ban Meta, Oakley Meta, or Snap Spectacles.
“It is completely unsurprising that people are building apps to fight back against Meta glasses and other surreptitious public recording,” Quintin told Ars. Many people “have a deep revulsion to being recorded without their consent, which is understandable,” and that remains “the biggest problem with these glasses,” Quintin said.
Smart-glasses detector apps aren’t perfect. At best, they can alert users when nearby glasses are turned on by detecting the Bluetooth signal used to pair the glasses with a phone. Most importantly, the apps cannot determine whether the glasses are actively recording, and users are cautioned to never assume that someone wearing smart glasses is recording them. App makers also advise against confrontation and accept no liability for false positives or misunderstandings. Additionally, detection may be unreliable if a wall or other obstacle, like a human body, interferes with a signal.
Users don’t seem to consider these flaws deal-breakers. They simply want some way to scan a room, and some are eager to provide feedback to improve the apps, even expressing an emotional investment in seeing the technology develop.
One of the first apps, Nearby Glasses, is available for $2.99 on both iOS and Android. It has been downloaded more than 100,000 times from the Play Store and remains the most popular such app, despite the developer, Yves Jeanrenaud, warning on GitHub that he’s “no pro developer” and that “detecting Bluetooth LE devices might sometimes just not work as expected,” and “false positives are likely.”
Released in response to online content showing that smart glasses are “an intolerable intrusion, consent neglecting, horrible piece of tech,” Jeanrenaud said, he kept his goals humble. On GitHub, he wrote that “I hope this app is useful for someone,” but “I do not want to promote techsolutionism, nor do I want people to feel falsely secure. It’s still an imperfect approach,” and it probably “always will be.”
By July, another detector, Antizuck Smart Glasses Scanner, was nearing the top of iPhone charts, also charging $3 for the service. One high school teacher reviewing the app called it the “best $3 I’ve spent,” writing that she was concerned that her students could use AI glasses to take unwanted recordings in class.
Ars tested the most recently released app, Zuckoff, which launched for free on iPhone in early August and is currently seeking 12 testers to launch on Android devices later this year.
Already, thousands of users have downloaded the iPhone app, with some eagerly submitting feedback that has helped improve key functionality, including the ability to detect AI glasses and receive alerts when the app is closed. Perpetual scanning is an optional feature that costs about $10 a year. The subscription helps cover the costs of “continuous support” for the app, Zuckoff’s creator, Pawel Szydlowski, told Ars.
Like Jeanrenaud’s app, Zuckoff collects no data and was created partly in response to toxic Meta glasses content flooding social media. Szydlowski told Ars that he built the app in one week after finishing another project that scans for nearby Bluetooth devices and deciding, “Let’s see how far we can go with detecting those glasses.”
Without researching whether other apps had already sought to solve the problem, Szydlowski decided to put his 10 years of iPhone developer experience to work. “I was like, ‘I can do something about it, so let’s go,’” Szydlowski told Ars.
Building a Meta glasses detector
Szydlowski’s biggest challenge was collecting the unique identifiers that manufacturers use to label different products for regulatory purposes. Zuckoff uses these identifiers to help users detect specific smart-glasses models while ignoring Bluetooth signals from less creepy devices. To compile as comprehensive a list as possible, Szydlowski crawled Instagram and Reddit for photos of people wearing different types of smart glasses.
“I see you have those glasses,” Szydlowski would say in messages to early Meta glasses adopters, who agreed to help despite presumably approving of the technology. “Can you help me with this little name? I want to know the unique identifier that’s broadcasting.”
To catch glasses with identifiers that Zuckoff hasn’t yet logged, Szydlowski created a workaround that first flags devices by their advertised names. It’s less precise, he said, but it gives users some indication that a pair of smart glasses may be nearby, even without a known identifier. He’s currently working on another solution that should widen discovery even further, he told Ars.
Szydlowski’s app first alerted him to nearby smart glasses when he ran into two colleagues wearing them at a recent Apple event in Poland. That helped him confirm the tech was working as he hoped.
When you load Zuckoff, the app “estimates distance from signal strength and puts a confidence level on every hit rather than a hard yes or no,” Szydlowski explained. Esitmates tell users if glasses are very close (within arm’s length), close (in the same room), near (nearby) and far. This feature also makes it possible to see when you may be approaching an area with a larger concentration of smart glasses, like in a tourist trap such as the Las Vegas strip.
Ars replicated the test, thanks to this writer’s brother-in-law, who agreed to use the app to detect his own Ray-Bans. He likes to use his smart glasses to record nature sightings when he goes boating or to take action shots of his bulldog playing fetch along the lake, and he had the glasses on him when I called to see if he could run the test.
After putting the glasses on, my brother-in-law loaded the app, which detected the glasses in minutes and warned that “one possible pair” was “within arm’s length.” (In this case, the message was very literal, since he was wearing the glasses while looking at the phone in his hand.)
The app then references the identifier to help the user detect exactly which model is nearby, and my brother-in-law confirmed that Zuckoff correctly labeled his smart glasses.
For Szydlowski, the toughest challenge was figuring out how Apple might allow the app to run in the background, since the company is “very strict when it comes to apps working in the background all the time.” He worried some users wouldn’t find the app as beneficial without that functionality. Eventually, he settled on a solution that scans continuously, but rather than flagging all known devices the moment they’re turned on, Apple allows only a fixed list of known Bluetooth service identifiers to be detected in that mode. Extra-cautious users should therefore also open the app to see the full list of potential devices in the area.
“This background feature, it’s so crucial,” Szydlowski said.
Android may allow him to offer faster detection through background functionality, Szydlowski suggested, because unlike Apple devices, Android allows background activities to be “possible to exempt from battery optimization,” Szydlowski said. That means Zuckoff “can continue using the battery in the background” without Android protocols that “wipe out the apps that are consuming your battery,” he said.
Although people have mostly grown accustomed to the idea of being recorded without consent in public, smart glasses have the potential to expand mass surveillance in ways that deeply concern privacy advocates.
Meta could introduce technical solutions, like automatically blurring faces, as Google does in Street View images, but Szydlowski doubts Meta would voluntarily make such a privacy-conscious change without regulatory or public pressure. The creator of Zuckoff, a name that takes a cheeky dig at Meta’s founder, also said that “I’m pretty sure they’re not going to be happy with this app existing.”
He likens malicious smart-glasses recording to the earliest harms of Apple’s AirTags. When that technology was released in 2021, the easy-to-hide tracking devices were soon implicated in stalking cases. But there still is no federal law targeting AirTag abuses, and it took the first states to act on the emerging privacy threat roughly three to five years to pass legislation prohibiting the invasive tracking.
Szydlowski worries lawmakers will be similarly slow to react to threats from Meta glasses. He told Ars he thinks the best solution might be rules mandating companies like Meta to advertise a specific Bluetooth service identifier while recording. That would improve civil defense apps like his.
In the meantime, he hopes people will find the detector app that they like best and use it to spread awareness of the risk that smart glasses may be present in a room where they’re unexpected or explicitly forbidden.
“The goal of this app was just making people aware because a lot of people won’t be aware until it becomes a major problem, which was the case with AirTags, basically,” Szydlowski said.
Meta expects demand to explode
Last December, analysts forecasted that 2026 would be a breakthrough year for smart glasses. And it’s clear by now that Meta wants this to be the year that AI glasses are suddenly everywhere you look.
The tech giant invested heavily in promoting them, collaborating with celebrity influencer Kylie Jenner on a pair of Ray-Bans featuring an AI assistant that speaks in her voice. The campaign featured billboard ads and a video spot showing Kylie simply enjoying wearing the glasses, without necessarily highlighting their practical features. The partnership was rumored to have paid Jenner millions of dollars and was intended to position the technology as a fashionable, practical accessory—and perhaps buff out the public perception of them as “pervert glasses.” But critics have argued that the ads seem narrowly designed to encourage more people to use their glasses for continuous recording.
Though the Jenner campaign was supposedly viewed as a success internally at Meta, it also prompted global backlash. On social media, the protest collective “Everyone Hates Elon” razed Jenner, The Huffington Post reported, saying that “recording everything we see and do constantly? It’s giving fascism, not fashion,” “hun.” And pop singer Lorde stopped a festival performance to tell her fans, “Fuck the glasses. Don’t get the glasses. Not sexy.”
Salon’s Andi Zeisler slammed the Kylie Edition glasses for trying to lull women into a false sense of security, even as Meta knows the technology has been used to record women without their knowledge, both in public and private. In London, activists took that criticism a step further, replacing bus stop ads of Jenner smiling in the glasses with a spoof in which her face transforms into a skeletal grin above the warning that at Meta, “We’re always watching.”
But despite protests, the glasses aren’t going away any time soon, as Meta plans to move millions more into production. In 2025, the company sold more than 7 million AI glasses—up from 2 million sold in the prior two years combined—then quickly made plans to double its Ray-Ban outputs, Bloomberg reported. By the end of 2026, Meta expects to start producing at least 20 million glasses annually to meet demand, or perhaps as many as 30 million if the market continues trending strongly.
Beyond the backlash, regulating the glasses is a touchy subject, Quintin told Ars. No civil rights group would advocate banning recording in public, a practice that can be crucial for holding police and government officials accountable. What may prove just as useful as thoughtful privacy regulations, Quintin suggested, is a broader effort to ban the technology at the community level.
Szydlowski told Ars that he’s personally not bothered by Meta’s AI glasses, only by the gross content made with them. But other critics, like Quintin, think the tech is “disgusting” and “unacceptable,” and he has little hope that technical solutions can solve the problem and abundant concern that the privacy risks will compound as enthusiasm for the technology grows.
Right now, there’s less social friction around using glasses to record than there was when people first started using phones to record public interactions, Quintin suggested. As a father of young children, he recently saw another dad using glasses to film kids at a birthday party, a moment that illustrates how smart glasses have shifted the power dynamic.
Previously, “if you wanted to record somebody, you had to take out your phone, shove it in their face,” Quintin said. “And they know they’re being recorded. That is a useful social friction. And the glasses remove that and put the friction on the other end. The friction is now on me, calling you a pervert for wearing glasses and telling you to stop recording my kids.”
Szydlowski somewhat agreed. He told Ars there’s value in being able to record hands-free from eye level, but he created Zuckoff because he draws the line at posting harmful smart-glasses recordings online.
“People are using it in a bad way,” Szydlowski said. “That was the first part that annoyed me. I was like, ‘I don’t like it. I just don’t enjoy the content, and I don’t think it’s valid’ because myself, I wouldn’t have a way to react to being recorded because I’m used to people holding the phone and actually pointing at me. Then I can say, ‘Hold on a second. This is not scrolling. Someone is actually recording.’”
Ashley is a senior policy reporter for Ars Technica, dedicated to tracking social impacts of emerging policies and new technologies. She is a Chicago-based journalist with 20 years of experience.

articles.title: NASA's ground control software has a worrying security flaw which could let hackers contact spacecraft
articles.text:
NASA's ground control software has a worrying security flaw which could let hackers contact spacecraft
Ground control to major hack
- NASA’s ground control software has a critical vulnerability that could allow third-party access to spacecraft
- The flaw has been found in a browser-based variant of NASA’s AMMOS Instrument Toolkit
- NASA has not publicly responded to the flaw’s disclosure
NASA’s open source ground control software has a critical vulnerability that could enable an unauthenticated attacker to gain access and take control of spacecraft. The AMMOS Instrument Toolkit’s browser-based interface is the source of the vulnerability, which has since been resolved.
The AIT-GUI (AMMOS Instrument Toolkit Graphical User Interface) tool up to version 2.5.1 has been identified as vulnerable, but the fault has been fixed in v2.5.2, according to researcher Yuval Elbar.
If the vulnerability had been found by a third party, it would have given access to issue commands to spacecraft, instruments, and execute server-side scripts. In addition, command sequences could potentially have been run by an attacker, leaving craft almost wholly beyond NASA’s control.
Weak API
Elbar, who works with the Cycode Agentic Development Security Platform, disclosed the vulnerability on August 18, 2026. The problem appears to start with AIT-GUI running as a web server with all network interfaces open, rather than the host’s setting. Incredibly, the API also has no authentication, or authorization protection. In addition, the CSRF (cross-site request forgery) protection on changing endpoints is also absent on affected versions of AIT-GUI.
Attackers can exploit basic access-control security failings in AIT-GUI, exposing the /cmd and /script/run and /seq prompts while also setting up filesystem paths. This enables files (potentially malware, or custom-built scripts) to be passed directly to NASA craft via a vulnerable AIT-GUI browser session, potentially escalating to full control.
To emphasize the scale of the weakness, Elbar introduced the disclosure with “A web GUI used to drive spacecraft and instrument commanding shipped a server that listens on every network interface, asks nobody for a password, and can be steered by any web page an operator happens to open.”
External access
As if this wasn’t concerning enough, the attacker doesn’t need to be on the same network. Direct access via an exposed port, or directing an operator to a web page hiding malicious code, or even simply a web page under live control by an attacker, can afford access to a third party.

Elbar adds “operational and ground-system software inherits the same web weaknesses as everything else, but with a far higher cost of failure. Auth, CSRF defense, and input confinement are not optional extras on a panel that commands hardware.”
Cycode advises administrators of AIT systems to upgrade AIT-GUI to v2.5.2 and run checks on the console port. They should also review command history.

articles.title: Trahie par de vieux boulons, Sophie Adenot est forcée de retourner dans le vide spatial
articles.text:
On ne laisse pas un travail à moitié fait dans l’espace. Après une première sortie extravéhiculaire (EVA) longue de plus de six heures le 18 août 2026, Sophie Adenot et son coéquipier américain Anil Menon vont devoir renfiler prochainement leur scaphandre de cosmonaute. La raison ? Leur opération de maintenance n’a pas pu être totalement achevée.
Précisément, Sophie Adenot et Anil Menon ont été confrontés à de vieux boulons très difficiles à dévisser, ce qui a ralenti significativement le rythme de l’intervention. Résultat, les réserves d’oxygène et de batterie se sont passablement épuisées avant d’en voir le bout. Et puis une telle sortie reste exigeante physiquement comme mentalement.
Il va donc falloir y retourner, et vite. L’agence spatiale américaine a annoncé le 20 août que le binôme effectuera une sortie complémentaire le 25 août, soit très exactement une semaine après le baptême du vide de Sophie Adenot — c’était en effet sa toute première EVA. Pour Anil, c’est presque la routine maintenant, car il s’agira de sa troisième sortie.
Ces activités de visserie visent à remplacer une antenne de communication de la Station spatiale internationale (ISS), afin d’en installer une nouvelle. Celle-ci avait été prépositionnée à l’extérieur du laboratoire orbital, au cours d’une précédente opération de ravitaillement, et stockée sur une plateforme, qui servira à ranger l’ancienne.
Comme à l’aller, ce « match retour » doit durer environ six heures et demie, et le duo reprendra là où il s’était arrêté.
La chorégraphie en impesanteur sera identique par ailleurs à ce que l’on a vu le 18 août : Anil Menon sera fixé à l’extrémité du grand bras robotique Canadarm2 pour récupérer l’antenne de rechange, tandis que Sophie Adenot sera le long de la structure, avec pour mission de la libérer de sa plateforme de stockage.
Les deux astronautes se retrouveront sur le segment de poutre Z1, situé au-dessus du module américain Unity, pour procéder aux branchements électriques et informatiques. Ils pourront encore compter sur leurs collègues restés à l’intérieur (Jessica Meir et Jack Hathaway) pour s’équiper avant de sortir, mais aussi piloter Canadarm2 et superviser l’opération.
Une mission bonus si le chrono le permet
Comme souvent avec la NASA, un planning serré n’empêche pas de prévoir du travail supplémentaire. Si l’installation de l’antenne se déroule sans accroc — et sans boulon capricieux cette fois —, le binôme s’attaquera à une mission « bonus » : le remplacement d’un rétro-réflecteur sur le module Harmony.
Ce composant, qui ne paye pas de mine, demeure essentiel pour l’ISS car il permet de fournir des données de navigation ultra-précises aux vaisseaux qui viennent s’amarrer à la station. C’est le genre d’équipement qui aide à éviter un mauvais rendez-vous spatial et, donc, une mauvaise manœuvre qui pourrait entraîner des complications.
Pour les passionnés qui suivront cette nouvelle aventure en direct le mardi 25 août (le début de la sortie est prévu vers 14h35, heure de Paris), la NASA a rappelé les codes couleurs pour distinguer les deux mécaniciens. Anil Menon portera un scaphandre orné de bandes rouges. Sophie Adenot sera quant à elle dans une combinaison blanche, sans marquage.
Enchaîner deux EVA en tout juste sept jours constitue un défi athlétique et mental certain, exigeant un effort musculaire durable et une concentration de chaque instant. Surtout pour une première pour la Française. Si elle vient à bout de ce marathon, l’astronaute marquera un peu plus l’histoire spatiale française, après être déjà devenue la première compatriote à effectuer ce type de sortie.

articles.title: Face à Netflix, YouTube sort le carnet de chèque pour ses plus gros créateurs
articles.text:
YouTube proposerait à certains de ses créateurs les plus populaires des contrats de plusieurs millions de dollars pour les inciter à ne pas céder leurs contenus à Netflix. Plusieurs accords seraient en cours de finalisation, mais aucun n’aurait encore été signé.
YouTube ne veut pas voir ses créateurs les plus populaires fuir vers la concurrence, y compris vers Netflix. Les offres du géant américain prendraient trois formes : un financement direct pour les émissions des créateurs, une part des partenariats publicitaires négociés par YouTube avec des marques, et des paiements anticipés. En échange, la plateforme exige des périodes d’exclusivité pendant lesquelles les contenus restent disponibles uniquement sur YouTube.
YouTube se met à choyer ses créateurs
Cette approche marque un changement pour une entreprise dont la relation avec les créateurs reposait jusqu’ici presque exclusivement sur un partage des revenus publicitaires. En finançant directement des émissions, YouTube adopte une logique plus proche de celle d’un studio de production que de celle d’une plateforme aux revenus passifs. Toutefois, il faut faire un choix dans les créateurs qui profitent de ces investissements.
Toutefois, YouTube ne serait pas tendre avec les créateurs qui mèneraient une "double vie" avec un concurrent. En effet, les créateurs ayant signé un contrat avec Netflix et YouTube en simultané, pourraient perdre l’accès aux campagnes marketing de YouTube, à ses événements majeurs et à une partie des partenariats publicitaires globaux. De quoi réfléchir à deux fois avant la signature d'un contrat.
Des stratégies totalement opposées
Ni YouTube ni Netflix n’ont commenté publiquement ces conditions, et les informations s’appuient sur des sources proches des négociations plutôt que sur des documents officiels. Contrairement à une exclusivité totale, YouTube ne demanderait qu’une période limitée d’exclusivité.
De son côté, Netflix adopte une stratégie inverse. Ses accords avec les créateurs YouTube sont des licences non exclusives, leur permettant de conserver leur chaîne, leurs revenus publicitaires, leurs partenariats et leurs produits dérivés. Le tout, en monétisant le droit de diffuser leur catalogue. Cette approche explique en partie son succès, un créateur sollicité pour un second revenu sans abandonner sa plateforme d’origine n’a aucune raison de refuser.
Plusieurs créateurs ont déjà signé avec Netflix
Depuis dix-huit mois, Netflix a signé plusieurs créateurs et podcasteurs, dont Ms. Rachel (début 2025), Mark Rober (août 2025), les Stokes Twins (juillet 2026), ainsi que les Sidemen, Rhett & Link, Jordan Matter et Nick DiGiovanni. La plateforme a aussi acquis des podcasts, comme celui de Jay Shetty via un accord de 100 millions de dollars avec Spotify, la plateforme aux 300 millions d'utilisateurs.
Netflix affirme que cette stratégie porte ses fruits. Dans son rapport semestriel What We Watched, la plateforme attribue à Ms. Rachel 126 millions de vues en une seule période, alors que ses vidéos restaient accessibles gratuitement sur YouTube.
L'enjeu n'est pas tant financier
Ces mouvements ne s’expliquent pas par un déclin de YouTube, dont le chiffre d’affaires a dépassé 60 milliards de dollars en 2025, un montant supérieur à celui de Netflix la même année. La plateforme indique avoir versé plus de 100 milliards de dollars aux créateurs sur quatre ans. L’enjeu n’est pas financier, mais attentionnel : YouTube doit convaincre les annonceurs qu’ils y trouveront leur audience. Un contenu également disponible sur Netflix affaiblit cet argument, même si la version YouTube conserve ses vues.
Par ailleurs, YouTube a récemment durci les conditions d’accès à son programme partenaire, doublant les seuils d’éligibilité. Les plateformes convergent vers une même logique : payer davantage, mais à un nombre restreint de créateurs.

articles.title: 1 000 km d’autonomie et recharge en 5 minutes : BYD au sommet avec son nouveau SUV électrique
articles.text:
La voiture électrique souffre toujours de défauts bien souvent psychologiques. Parmi eux, ce sont l’autonomie et la recharge qui figurent en tête. À juste titre si l’on remonte dans les années 2010 : les modèles les plus populaires que furent les Renault Zoé et Nissan Leaf souffraient d’une polyvalence absolument ridicule. 16 ans plus tard, les moqueries n’ont clairement plus lieu d’être avec les progrès spectaculaires des véhicules à batterie.
Finie la panne sèche : quand l’électrique enterre le thermique
BYD nous fait une démonstration de force avec son nouveau SUV tiré de sa marque premium Denza. Le N8 est en ce sens un véritable monstre en la matière qui pourrait convaincre les derniers réfractaires. L’autonomie n’est plus du tout un problème avec un rayon d’action homologué à 1 003 km sur le cycle CLTC. Ramené à du WLTP, on dépassera sans crainte les 700 km d’autonomie, de quoi dissiper toutes les contraintes à ce sujet.
1 003 km d’autonomie : le pari fou de BYD
BYD affirme d’ailleurs que les 1 003 km d’autonomie constituent « un record mondial dans la catégorie ». C’est fou à dire, mais le rayon d’action devient similaire à un modèle équivalent alimenté au sans-plomb, ce qui veut bien dire que l’électrique a rattrapé le thermique. Bien sûr, le diesel garde encore une petite avance sur ce point, mais au prix d’un agrément de conduite largement inférieur.
Une batterie XXL dans un gabarit XXL
Avouons que le bruit, les vibrations et la réactivité d’un mazout sont difficiles à avaler après avoir goûté à l’électrique. La performance a été rendue possible par la batterie Blade 2.0 d’une capacité XXL de 130,15 kWh. Le pack est alors aussi énorme que le véhicule, qui mesure 5,15 mètres de long, 2 mètres de large et 1,82 mètre de haut. Un véritable camion, dont l’intérieur princier n’a pas été dévoilé.
5 minutes de charge : mission presque accomplie face à l’essence
L’autre point spectaculaire que BYD a forcément rendu public est la recharge : avec une puissance en pic de 1 500 kW en courant continu DC, le Denza N8 explose tous les records. De quoi passer de 10 à 70 % de batterie en seulement 5 minutes. Quant à la recharge complète de 10 à 97 %, elle ne réclame que 9 minutes. De quoi presque égaler le ravitaillement d’un modèle essence ou diesel.
Une bête de course… qu’on ne verra probablement pas chez nous
Seule condition, trouver les bornes Flash Charger de BYD, encore rares en Europe, mais de plus en plus présentes en Chine. Les puissances sont tout aussi délirantes avec au choix 435 ou 503 ch en propulsion et jusqu’à 1 210 ch en transmission intégrale avec trois moteurs. Sommes-nous fichus ? Clairement pas, car le Denza N8 n’est pour l’instant pas prévu en Europe. Contentons-nous de la Z9GT, déjà rendue hors de prix par les taxes…

articles.title: A qué temperatura poner el aire acondicionado si afuera hay 35°C
articles.text:
Cuando la temperatura exterior en verano alcanza los 35°C, surge una pregunta recurrente en muchos hogares: ¿a cuántos grados se debe programar el aire acondicionado para lograr un ambiente confortable sin que el consumo energético se dispare?
Según la Organización de Consumidores y Usuarios de España (OCU), existe una medida clave: mantener una diferencia de unos 8°C respecto al exterior es la mejor estrategia para equilibrar confort y coste eléctrico. Esto significa que si el termómetro en la calle llega a 35°C, lo óptimo será ajustar el aire acondicionado a 27°C.
PUBLICIDAD
Esta pauta busca reducir la factura de la luz y minimizar el impacto ambiental, sin renunciar a una sensación térmica agradable en el interior de la casa.
Por qué no se debe bajar más la temperatura del aire acondicionado
La OCU explica que reducir la temperatura por debajo de ese umbral no acelera el enfriamiento: “Ajustar el aire a 17°C no consigue que la habitación se enfríe más rápido. El aparato tardará lo mismo en alcanzar los 24°C y después seguirá funcionando hasta llegar a la temperatura programada, incrementando el gasto eléctrico”.
PUBLICIDAD
Cada grado adicional de enfriamiento supone un aumento mínimo del 7% en el consumo energético del aparato, un dato muy relevante en temporadas de uso intensivo como en verano.
Además, programar el aire a temperaturas muy bajas puede ocasionar molestias físicas y generar diferencias térmicas excesivas con el exterior, lo que afecta a la sensación de confort y puede contribuir al desperdicio energético.
PUBLICIDAD
Qué funciones del aire acondicionado permiten enfriar más rápido una habitación
Para quienes buscan una refrigeración rápida, la OCU sugiere utilizar las funciones “Turbo” o “Power cool”, disponibles en muchos aparatos modernos. Estas opciones, aunque suelen aumentar el ruido y pueden ser menos eficientes, son útiles cuando se necesita acondicionar el ambiente en poco tiempo.
La clave está en no bajar la temperatura de referencia, sino activar estas funciones específicas para lograr el objetivo sin comprometer la eficiencia a largo plazo.
PUBLICIDAD
La OCU advierte que estas funcionalidades deben emplearse de manera puntual, porque su uso prolongado puede afectar el rendimiento del electrodoméstico y elevar el coste energético.
“Si tienes prisa por enfriar, usa las funciones de refrigeración rápida, pero recuerda volver a la configuración óptima para mantener el consumo bajo control”, dice la OCU.
PUBLICIDAD
Por qué es clave limpiar los filtros del aire acondicionado
El mantenimiento del aire acondicionado es un aspecto que suele pasar desapercibido. La OCU señala que un filtro obstruido puede aumentar el consumo de energía entre un 5 y un 15%. Realizar una limpieza y revisión anual garantiza que el sistema funcione de manera eficiente y prolonga la vida útil del aparato.
La organización compara el mantenimiento del aire acondicionado con el de una caldera antes de la llegada del frío. “Limpiar los filtros hará que el sistema funcione de manera más eficiente”, subraya la OCU.
PUBLICIDAD
Si se descuida esta tarea, el electrodoméstico trabajará con mayor esfuerzo para alcanzar la temperatura deseada, lo que se traduce en un gasto adicional de energía y una posible reducción del confort.
Qué otras formas hay para refrescar la casa
Frente al impulso de encender el aire acondicionado, la OCU recuerda la eficacia de los ventiladores. Estos aparatos, mucho más económicos tanto en la compra como en el consumo, pueden costar menos de 15 euros durante todo el verano si se usan diez horas al día, mientras que el aire acondicionado puede elevar la factura en alrededor de 300 euros.
PUBLICIDAD
Aunque un ventilador no reduce la temperatura ambiente, sí favorece la evaporación del sudor y genera una mayor sensación de frescor. Los ventiladores de techo, en particular, pueden mejorar el confort térmico.
Asimismo, se debe combinar el uso de ventiladores con el cierre adecuado de puertas y ventanas para evitar que el aire frío se escape, y, en caso necesario, usar burletes o soluciones temporales como toallas.

articles.title: Google's AI coding agent just escaped its own IDE
articles.text:
Google’s AI coding agent just escaped its own IDE
When Google launched Antigravity in November 2025, it was on the premise that developers could hand an entire coding task to an AI agent and let it run. But developers still need to work directly in their code editor.
Google announced Thursday that it is expanding Antigravity into developers’ existing workflows through new extensions for Visual Studio Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains IDEs and Zed. The company is also making Antigravity available through eligible Gemini Enterprise subscriptions.
The extensions let developers open agent conversations in a side panel, review inline diffs, inspect plans and delegate multi-step engineering tasks without moving a project into the Antigravity 2.0 desktop application. The same Antigravity account works across each environment, so users don’t have to sign in or manage licenses separately.
Agents inside every IDE
The VS Code extension is available now via Microsoft’s extension marketplace on macOS, Linux, and Windows, while the extension for Visual Studio 2026 and .NET solutions is currently in preview. Google is also supporting the JetBrains suite (including IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, WebStorm, GoLand, CLion, and Rider) starting with version 2026.2.1, alongside Zed.
Meeting developers in their editor of choice makes it far easier for Google to land inside enterprise engineering teams, where people rarely use the exact same setup.
Enterprise budgets and guardrails
Admins can turn on Google’s developer tools for employees on Gemini Enterprise Standard, Plus or Standard Emerging Market plans. They can also cap monthly spending for each Google Cloud project. When the included quota runs out, Antigravity either shuts off or switches to pay-as-you-go pricing. Google says controls for individual users and teams are coming later this year.
Until then, everyone in the same edition, project, and region draws from a single pool of credits. Google explains the allowance as monthly but meters it using a rolling seven-day pool. Anything left disappears when the pool resets.
A nontrivial engineering task can consume 150,000 to 200,000 tokens, while multi-agent handoffs add more input tokens each time work passes between agents.
Token spending spirals quickly
That quota can go quickly. A nontrivial engineering task can consume 150,000 to 200,000 tokens, while multi-agent handoffs add more input tokens each time work passes between agents. One built-in Claude Code skill was recently found to be loading more than 200,000 tokens before answering a question. Without a default allocation for each developer, an agent-heavy workflow could burn through the team’s entire pool within hours.
Google is not the first vendor to confront this problem. Microsoft recently introduced AI token budgets for its engineering divisions after discovering that many of its engineers were spending hundreds to thousands of dollars per month on tokens. Uber reportedly exhausted its entire 2026 AI coding budget in the first four months of the year. An internal Amazon project meant to match author records with product listings exceeded its planned budget by 860%.
Security policies follow authentication
Enterprise developers sign in with their company credentials, then choose the Google Cloud project and region Antigravity should use. Organizations can connect to their existing identity provider via Workforce Identity Federation, while developers can also authenticate using Application Default Credentials.
Once authenticated, agent sessions inherit the organization’s IAM policies, VPC Service Controls and regional data boundaries. Google says data from enterprise Antigravity sessions is not used to train its foundation models.
Once one of those connections reaches a production system, a bad setting can have serious consequences.
Admins can limit an agent’s workspace, block browser access, and decide which MCP servers it can use. Once one of those connections reaches a production system, a bad setting can have serious consequences. ElevenLabs’ MCP server, for example, let Claude delete production voice agents from a chat window. A connection with that kind of power needs to be treated like any other privileged access.
Putting Antigravity inside existing editors lets Google get its agents onto developers’ machines without requiring a company-wide tooling change, while Gemini Enterprise keeps every session tied to the same policies and project budget regardless of whether it starts in VS Code or JetBrains. Developers can switch editors without changing what the agent can reach or how its usage is billed.
The extension gets Antigravity through the door; the control plane determines what it can do once it is inside.

articles.title: AI skills in cybersecurity job postings doubled as junior hiring stalls - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
AI skills in cybersecurity job postings doubled as junior hiring stalls
The AI Workforce Consortium today reported that the share of cybersecurity job postings across the Group of Seven economies that ask for artificial intelligence skills doubled over the year, and junior hiring has not moved with them.
This was the first in a new series of spotlight reports, this one on the impact of AI agents on cybersecurity. Job demand across the G7 grew 9.5% in the six months through March, measured against the same period a year earlier. The preceding half-year came in at 6.8%.
AI skills turned up in 28.5% of those postings, against 14.2% a year before. The most recent month in the data ran at 29.7%. All of it covers G7 markets only.
Sort the same postings by seniority and the picture changes. Senior-titled roles grew 65% in the six months through March. Growth in junior-titled roles was 5.9%. In the half-year before that they had shrunk slightly. The consortium calls this the experience paradox. Employers are asking for senior skills in jobs that are nominally entry level.
Cisco Systems Inc., which founded the consortium, asked security leaders what they cannot find in entry-level candidates. Hands-on experience with AI agents was the top gap, at 49%. Technical cybersecurity depth was 48%, human skills 45%. Four percentage points separate the top and bottom of that list, so the three are presented as a cluster rather than a ranking.
The same survey asked about budgets. Leaders picked up to three investment priorities for the next two years, and AI-powered defense was chosen most often, by 36%. People came fourth on 25%, level with threat intelligence.
Anthropic PBC disclosed a cyber-espionage campaign in November 2025 in which its Claude model ran 80% to 90% of the operation under limited human direction. In early July, Sysdig Inc. documented a fully autonomous ransomware operation.
Two weeks after that came an intrusion at Hugging Face Inc. run end to end by an autonomous agent system. OpenAI Group PBC later said said two of its models were involved, one of them unreleased. Cyber refusals had been reduced on both for an internal evaluation.
The Five Eyes cybersecurity agencies issued a joint warning on frontier models on June 22. “The timeline is not years, it is months,” they wrote.
Roles are being rebuilt around that shift. The tier-one security operations center analyst is the clearest case. That job was manual triage. It is now closer to supervising agents and checking their work. Digital forensics analyst was the fastest-growing title in the posting analysis, up 453%, though from a base of roughly 150 to 200 AI-skilled forensics listings per half-year.
“One of the roles that is getting reshaped the fastest is the tier 1 SOC analyst,” Omar Santos, a distinguished engineer at Cisco, said during a consortium webinar in May. Triage, threat intelligence checks and data correlation are “where agentic systems are now generally effective,” he said. “Everybody is an orchestrator now.”
Ethical reasoning showed up in 533% more cybersecurity listings than a year earlier. Systems thinking was up 251%. Stakeholder engagement, 125%. The bases are small in all three cases, and the authors treat the numbers as direction rather than a measure of market size.
IBM Corp.’s Cost of a Data Breach Report 2025 found 63% of breached organizations either had no AI governance policy or were still writing one. One in five reported a breach involving tools staff had adopted outside official channels. Organizations with high levels of shadow AI carried about $670,000 in additional breach cost.
Kyu Kwak, chief information security officer at Pearson plc, said the organizations that succeed will be the ones with “the strongest governance around autonomous systems.”
Employers are paying for the skills they say they cannot find. In Lightcast data cited by the consortium, U.S. cybersecurity jobs that require AI skills advertise a median salary 14.9% higher than the field overall.
Cisco set up the consortium in 2024, then called the AI-Enabled ICT Workforce Consortium, with nine other companies, among them Accenture plc, Google LLC and Microsoft Corp. Pearson joined this year, taking it to 11. The combined upskilling target is now 130 million people over the next decade.
A second spotlight report, on governing AI, is next.
Image: AI Workforce Consortium

articles.title: G.Skill starts paying buyers $20 to $25 from $2.4 million settlement over misleading RAM speeds
articles.text:
Winners & losers: G.Skill has started paying customers who joined a $2.4 million class action settlement over claims that it misled buyers about the speeds of its DDR4 and DDR5 memory. Those set to receive payouts shouldn't start shopping for a yacht, though: claimants are receiving around $20 to $25.
The payments began landing this week, six months after the settlement was announced. Screenshots shared online show one claimant receiving $19.68 through Zelle, while two others reportedly received $24.60 each. As is usually the case with class actions, the amount depends on how many valid claims were filed and the number of qualifying products each person purchased.
The settlement administrator began issuing payments on August 18, following final court approval on June 9. The deadline to submit a claim passed on April 7, so anyone who forgot to file is out of luck.
The lawsuit, filed in 2022, accused G.Skill of deceptively advertising desktop DDR4 and DDR5 modules at speeds they couldn't achieve out of the box (i.e., they needed to be overclocked).
Also read: Testing AMD's EXPO Ultra Low Latency Memory
The plaintiffs argued that buyers were not clearly told they would need to enable an overclocking profile or adjust BIOS settings to reach the figures printed on the packaging.
Modern memory kits usually boot using conservative JEDEC settings. Hitting their advertised speeds often requires enabling Intel's XMP or AMD's EXPO, while the maximum stable speed also depends on the processor's integrated memory controller and the motherboard. This is something most PC enthusiasts understand, but the case centered on whether the distinction was made sufficiently clear to less experienced buyers.
The settlement covers US residents who purchased non-laptop G.Skill DDR4 products rated above 2,133 MHz or DDR5 products rated above 4,800 MHz between January 31, 2018, and January 7, 2026. Claimants could include up to five purchases per household without receipts, but proof was required for additional products.
G.Skill denied wrongdoing and maintained that its memory was correctly labeled and performed as advertised. Settling allowed the company to end the litigation without a court deciding whether it violated consumer protection laws or breached express warranties.
In addition to the payouts, G.Skill agreed to change its packaging, product pages, and specifications supplied to retailers. Rated speeds will be described as "up to" figures, accompanied by a warning that overclocking or BIOS adjustments are required and that maximum performance depends on the motherboard and CPU.
Of the $2.4 million fund, up to $800,000 was allocated to attorneys' fees and $295,000 to administration. Earlier court filings estimated that about $1.17 million would remain for buyers, which is why the payments aren't going to fund anyone's next high-end memory upgrade.

articles.title: Samsung marca evento em 27 de agosto; Galaxy S26 FE deve ser destaque • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Samsung marca evento em 27 de agosto; Galaxy S26 FE deve ser destaque
Apresentação começa às 9h, no horário de Brasília, com transmissão pelo YouTube.
Resumo
- Samsung confirmou o evento para revelar um novo celular da família Galaxy S, no dia 27 de agosto às 9h.
- As informações indicam que o modelo a ser apresentado será o novo Galaxy S26 FE.
- O aparelho pode chegar ao mercado com chip Exynos 2500, bateria de 4.900 mAh e certificação IP68.
A Samsung confirmou um novo evento focado na linha Galaxy para a próxima quinta-feira (27/08), às 9h no horário de Brasília. Segundo a fabricante, a apresentação irá revelar o “mais novo integrante da família Galaxy S26”. As informações até aqui indicam que será o Galaxy S26 FE.
O novo membro da linha Fan Edition deve manter a tradição de oferecer dispositivos posicionados um degrau acima dos intermediários, entregando recursos premium em um pacote mais acessível. O antecessor Galaxy S25 FE chegou ao Brasil por R$ 5.499, em setembro do ano passado.
Galaxy S26 FE pode trazer o Exynos 2500
O modelo pode chegar ao mercado equipado com o processador Exynos 2500 em conjunto com uma bateria de 4.900 mAh. Conforme antecipado pelo Android Headlines, o dispositivo virá com tela plana AMOLED de 6,7 polegadas. O display deve oferecer resolução Full HD+ e taxa de atualização de 120 Hz, com um recorte centralizado para a câmera de selfies.
Em construção, o celular apareceu nos vazamentos com moldura de alumínio, vidro Gorilla Glass Victus+ na tela e certificação IP68 contra poeira e submersão em água. Segundo o material, o dispositivo terá três opções de cores: Blueberry (azul), Graphite (grafite) e Pistachio (verde).
O que esperar das câmeras e recursos de software?
O módulo fotográfico traseiro pode manter a identidade visual da Samsung, com as três lentes alinhadas verticalmente. O vazamento indica um sensor principal de 50 megapixels, complementado por uma câmera ultrawide de 12 megapixels e uma teleobjetiva de 8 megapixels. Na parte frontal, as selfies e videochamadas ficariam por conta de uma câmera de 12 megapixels.
Em termos de software, o conteúdo de marketing confirma recursos nativos do Galaxy AI para captura e edição, incluindo as funções Bloqueio Horizontal, Apagador de Áudio e My FanCam, e sete anos de suporte, cobrindo tanto as atualizações do Android quanto os pacotes de segurança.
Como assistir ao evento da Samsung online?
O evento está oficialmente agendado para começar às 9h, pelo horário de Brasília. A transmissão acontecerá ao vivo, pelo site oficial da Samsung ou por meio do canal da empresa no YouTube.

articles.text:
Got a new Google Pixel 11 Pro XL? Here are the phone cases and covers that won't let you down
Take that dodgy, cheap case out of your basket — your phone deserves better
On the hunt for a Google Pixel 11 Pro XL case? I'm here to help. I've sifted through the sea of options on the market to find the options that will actually keep your phone protected — and looking good at the same time. You'll find my top picks in the US and in the UK below.
The Pixel 11 Pro XL is one of the new models announced in August 2026. The Pro XL is the big-screen option, with a 6.8-inch display. It sits alongside the standard Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro, both of which have a 6.3-inch screen. (We've tried them all out, and were impressed.) If you haven't yet made your phone purchase, our Pixel 11 series deals roundup will point you to the best places to buy one.
Back to the cases, though. Amazon is inundated with cheap, no-brand options, which might be fine for a bit, but if you want to get serious about protecting your phone it's worth paying a bit more for a trusted brand. Spigen, Mous and OtterBox are all known for quality and reliability, and all are available via Amazon as well as though their own sites. For quirky designs, my go-to is CASETiFY, and for leather covers and wallet-style cases, take a look at Snakehive. articles.title: AVerMedia Unveils High-Performance Capture Solutions for Next-Gen Livestreaming
articles.text:
Thursday, August 20th 2026
	
	
	
	
AVerMedia Unveils High-Performance Capture Solutions for Next-Gen Livestreaming
AVerMedia Technologies, a global leader in digital audiovisual solutions, today announced the GC531 and GC535, two professional-grade HDMI capture devices designed for hardcore streamers, live and video commerce operators, and professional video workflows. Whether paired with a DSLR or mirrorless camera, both devices enable high-quality and reliable video streaming and recording.
"Streamers today expect more than just a capture device. They need solutions that can grow with their workflow and adapt to evolving production requirements," said Michael Kuo, CEO of AVerMedia Technologies. "AVerMedia offers one of the industry's most comprehensive streaming ecosystems, providing a clear upgrade path from entry-level streaming to professional production. With the GC531 and GC535, creators gain professional-grade reliability, true color capture, and the flexibility to scale their production with confidence."As video becomes a critical component of communication, training, live production, and digital commerce, organizations increasingly require capture solutions that deliver not only image quality, but also long-term reliability, compatibility, and operational stability. Designed to meet these demands, the GC531 and GC535 provide dependable video capture for both everyday workflows and mission-critical environments.
Designed for 24/7 Live Commerce, professional video commerce, and Color-Critical Workflows
As video commerce continues to expand worldwide, brands, retailers, and creators are investing in higher-quality live productions to better engage with audiences and showcase products. Success in these environments depends not only on visual quality, but also on stable, reliable streaming performance during extended broadcasting sessions.
Designed for professional camera workflows, the GC535 and GC531 capture cards deliver accurate color reproduction, dependable operation, and broad camera compatibility. Whether for live selling, product demonstrations, training sessions, or content creation, they help businesses present products with clarity and confidence while maintaining uninterrupted streaming performance.
In addition, both models support RGB24 True Color Capture, enabling more accurate color reproduction and finer image details than conventional compressed capture formats. This is particularly valuable for live commerce applications, where product appearance directly influences customers' trust and purchasing decisions. By faithfully reproducing colors, fabrics, cosmetics, and other visual details, RGB24 helps enhance products appear as intended, fostering buyer confidence while reducing potential disputes and returns. The GC535 supports up to 4K30 RGB24 capture, while the GC531 supports up to 2K30 RGB24 capture.
Beyond exceptional image quality, the GC531 and GC535 are crafted for seamless professional deployment. Both capture cards offer broad compatibility with leading broadcast cameras and production workflows, enabling effortless integration into existing studio setups. To meet the demands of mission-critical streaming, both models feature enhanced EMC/EMI shielding and ESD protection to safeguard signal integrity, while rigorous long-duration reliability testing guarantees unwavering stability during continuous, 24/7 broadcasts.
For organizations that depend on uninterrupted video workflows, the GC531 and GC535 deliver the image quality, reliability, and operational stability required for professional streaming and mission-critical applications.
Product Availability
The GC531 and GC535 will be available globally through AVerMedia's official store, major retailers, and online platforms starting August 20, 2026.

articles.title: Rocket Report: SpaceX makes its mark on the Moon; ULA names new boss
articles.text:
NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter captured this view of a fresh crater created August 5 by the impact of a Falcon 9 upper stage on the Moon.
Credit:
NASA/Goddard Space Flight Center/Intuitive Machines
Welcome to Edition 9.07 of the Rocket Report! China’s workhorse Long March rocket family appears to be rebounding quickly from a rare launch failure August 10. Chinese officials have not publicly released any information on what may have caused the Long March 7A rocket to break apart less than 90 seconds after liftoff, but the rocket’s use of YF-100 engines initially raised questions about the failure’s impact on other Chinese rockets that use the same type of engines. But no biggie. YF-100 engines returned to flight six days later with the successful flight of a Long March 12 rocket, and the heavy-lift Long March 5—also with YF-100 engines—is set to launch in a few days with one of China’s most important space missions of the decade: the Chang’e 7 lunar lander en route to the Moon’s south pole.
As always, we welcome reader submissions. If you don’t want to miss an issue, please subscribe using the box below (the form will not appear on AMP-enabled versions of the site). Each report will include information on small-, medium-, and heavy-lift rockets, as well as a quick look ahead at the next three launches on the calendar.
Trouble in Taiwan. A prototype for a future satellite launch vehicle developed by Taiwan’s top weapons manufacturer veered off course shortly after liftoff Wednesday, Taiwan’s Central News Agency reports. The “trajectory anomaly” prompted the activation of the rocket’s self-destruct mechanism. The government agency responsible for the test flight, the National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology (NCSIST), reported no injuries or property damage. Debris from rocket fell into a planned safety control zone near the southern tip of Taiwan.
Parallel paths… Details about Wednesday’s rocket test are scarce, but the flight likely involved a sub-scale suborbital version of NCSIST’s planned military satellite launcher. The launch was the first test flight for the military’s satellite launch program, which focuses on developing a solid-fueled rocket to place small payloads into low-Earth orbit. At the same time, the civilian Taiwan Space Agency is developing a liquid-fueled satellite launcher that could be ready for orbital missions in the early 2030s.
The Ars Technica Rocket Report
The easiest way to keep up with Eric Berger’s and Stephen Clark’s reporting on all things space is to sign up for our newsletter. We’ll collect their stories and deliver them straight to your inbox.
Second failure for South Korea’s Innospace. A small suborbital rocket owned by South Korean startup Innospace lost control Thursday seconds into a test flight from Brazil’s Alcântara Space Center, the company said in a statement. The Brazilian Air Force, which runs the spaceport, activated the Sebit rocket’s flight termination system after it deviated from the planned trajectory. Innospace said there were no injuries or property damage. “While we regret that the planned flight could not be fully completed, the test flight provided valuable flight data from key systems, including the launch pad, propulsion system, and guidance, navigation and control (GNC),” Innospace said.
Hard times… Sebit is a “multipurpose suborbital rocket” designed to carry payloads up to 100 kilometers (62 miles) altitude, the boundary between Earth’s atmosphere and space. This was the second consecutive failure for Innospace, which attempted its first orbital launch from the same Brazilian spaceport in December. In a similar outcome to this week’s launch, Innospace’s Hanbit-Nano orbital rocket spun out of control seconds after liftoff.
Satellite operators fear launch crisis. SpaceX’s success with the Falcon 9 rocket helped open new avenues to orbit for a host of satellite startups. But the Falcon 9 may soon go away. SpaceX is eager to retire it in favor of the much larger, still unproven Starship rocket. This has led to consternation in the commercial satellite industry, Ars reports. There are growing concerns that SpaceX will largely focus on its own payloads—Starlink V3 satellites and orbital data centers—because of their potential to drive far greater profits. The Starship rocket’s Pez satellite dispenser, optimized for Starlink, is an indication of the company’s priorities.
Coming soon… SpaceX’s Gwynne Shotwell has previously said the operational lifetime of the Falcon 9 may end in 2030 or 2032. However, more recently, commercial satellite customers have been running into difficulties when trying to purchase a launch after 2028. One source said SpaceX has told the US government that it intends to end commercial launches after 2028 but will continue flying the Falcon 9 rocket for a limited number of federally contracted missions after that. Whether or not these dates stick, it has become clear to commercial satellite operators that they can no longer reliably plan their future around the workhorse Falcon 9.
Ukraine strikes Russian rocket factory. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed on Saturday that his country struck the Progress Rocket Space Center deep within Russia using ground-launched cruise missiles, Ars reports. “In Russia’s Samara region, one of the key enterprises within Roscosmos—the Progress Center, which was involved, among other things, in electronics production–was hit,” Zelenskyy said on X. “Flamingo missiles were used. A good achievement.”
Soyuz in the crosshairs… The largest city in the Samara Oblast, about 900 km from the Ukrainian border, Samara is home to Russia’s most important manufacturer of rockets. The Progress Center assembles the workhorse vehicle for Russia, the Soyuz-2 vehicle, as well as the newer Soyuz-5 rocket. The facility also builds military satellites. Russia uses the Soyuz-2 rocket, which has a lift capacity of about 8 metric tons to low-Earth orbit, for various civil and military purposes. Notably, it is the principal rocket used for Russia’s human spacecraft launches, raising questions about spillover effects for the International Space Station.
There’s now a second reusable Chinese rocket. It has been a little more than a month since China recovered an orbital-class rocket booster for the first time. A second launch operator accomplished a similar feat Tuesday in another sign of China’s growing launch capability, Ars reports. The Zhuque-3 rocket, developed by an 11-year-old company named LandSpace, lifted off from China’s Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center on Tuesday. The medium-lift rocket successfully placed a single satellite into low-Earth orbit, and its first stage booster returned to an on-target landing downrange in the Gobi Desert. This was the second flight of LandSpace’s Zhuque-3 rocket. The booster crash landed on the first Zhuque-3 flight last December.
Deep bench… LandSpace’s achievement this week follows the successful recovery of a Chinese Long March 10B booster in July. Several more Chinese companies seem poised to attempt booster landings in the next few months. None of China’s space companies—even the country’s colossal state-owned enterprises—can come close to matching SpaceX’s rapid-fire launch schedule. Collectively, they only launch about half as often as SpaceX. But that is with a fleet of entirely expendable rockets. China’s foray into the realm of reusable rockets could change that.
Charting America’s launch dominance. New research is beginning to quantify just how much the introduction of SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rocket, the adoption of reuse, and the vehicle’s high cadence have upended the global launch market, Ars reports. One of the more striking findings by public policy researchers based in the United Kingdom and Italy, based on new research published in Economics Letters, comes in the cumulative payload to orbit by nation. Russia and the United States tracked fairly close to one another for decades. That began to change in the last 10 years, and amid the Falcon 9 ramp up in the early 2020s, the United States has pulled ahead dramatically.
Reuse or bust… SpaceX has also made significant gains in controlling costs compared to other nations, thanks to reusable rockets. A decade ago, the United States and Europe had similar launch costs. Today, according to publicly available data, launch costs in Europe are now three times higher than for comparable payloads in the United States. The researchers estimate that the average cost of sending a kilogram of payload to orbit in the United States is now $3,225, compared to higher costs elsewhere: Japan ($5,287), China ($5,809), Russia ($6,682), and Europe ($9,897). India is higher still at nearly $15,000 a kilogram.
Au revoir to Ariane 6 Block 3. The European Space Agency is no longer considering the Ariane 6 Block 3 evolution, an upgrade that would have introduced a new upper stage made of carbon-fiber reinforced plastic to replace heavier legacy metallic structures, European Spaceflight reports. An ESA spokesperson said development continues on technologies for Ariane 6 Block 2, some of which have already started flying (larger solid rocket boosters). An orbital transfer vehicle, or kick stage, named Astris will become available as an add-on for Ariane 6 missions around 2029. But ESA has halted work on the new lightweight Icarus upper stage after the project failed to win support from ESA member states.
Tightening the screws… The first public indication of the death of Ariane 6 Block 3 came from SpaceScout, which reported earlier this month on a presentation from ESA scientists on a proposed robotic mission to orbit and land on Saturn’s moon Enceladus. The team developing the mission said they are reassessing their design, which previously assumed the availability of Ariane 6 Block 3 for launch in the 2030s.
SpaceX’s new scar on the Moon. New images from NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter show the aftermath from the impact of a spent Falcon 9 rocket body on the Moon. NASA released the images this week, showing a fresh impact scar near Einstein Crater, located on the western limb of the Moon as seen from Earth. LRO’s narrow-angle camera captured a view of the Falcon 9 upper stage’s impact site at multiple angles, revealing a new crater approximately 60 feet in diameter and less than 10 feet deep. The rocket left flying in deep space after launching a commercial Moon lander in 2025.
A learning opportunity… The rare, but not unprecedented, collision between an abandoned rocket and the Moon offered a chance for some unexpected research. The impact excavated pristine materials from below the lunar surface that have escaped weathering from the solar wind, galactic cosmic rays, and micrometeorites. It also provided an opportunity for asteroid trackers on Earth to refine their methods for impact predictions. It turns out their predictions of the Falcon 9’s impact site was accurate to about 0.6 miles, according to NASA.
Starship recovered from Indian Ocean. SpaceX’s most recent Starship test flight may have ended July 24, but its mission isn’t over yet. The spacecraft unexpectedly remained intact after splashdown in the Indian Ocean last month, prompting SpaceX officials to come up with an ad hoc plan to recover the vehicle. Over 24 days, a recovery ship towed the spacecraft engines-first several hundred miles to the Australian territory of Christmas Island. From there, SpaceX hopes to find a way to bring the spacecraft back to the company’s home base in South Texas.
Hardware rich… Engineers have reams of data from all 13 test flights of Starship and its giant booster rocket, known as the Super Heavy. But there’s no match for inspecting hardware after returning from space. SpaceX routinely recovers and reuses Falcon 9 booster stages with near-flawless performance. The handful of minor failures with the Falcon 9 have centered on the rocket’s single-use upper stage. So, getting Starship back in one piece is a boon. Engineers are particularly interesting in inspecting the ship’s heat shield as they hone in on a design for full and rapid reusability.
China will soon launch an ambitious Moon mission. As soon as this Sunday, a Long March 5 rocket will launch from a coastal seaport in China, carrying the Chang’e 7 lunar exploration mission, Ars reports. This is the latest and most sophisticated mission in China’s successful lunar exploration program, which dates back nearly two decades. The mission will pack a punch: It contains a lunar orbiter with high-resolution cameras and other sophisticated tools, a lunar lander, a lunar rover, and a mini-hopper of a probe. Although the lander’s mass has not been disclosed publicly, it is several times larger than the NASA-backed probes that have recently landed on the Moon, such as Firefly’s Blue Ghost.
Location, location, location… But what is most notable about Chang’e 7 is where the probe is going. It will land near one of the most compelling regions of the Moon, Shackleton Crater, very nearly at the south pole. Much of the lunar surface is pretty barren, but the south pole, and Shackleton Crater in particular, offers some of the most coveted real estate there. This is because the high rims of the crater create permanently shadowed regions known as “cold traps,” where it’s thought that water (in the form of ice, of course) and other useful materials may have accumulated over billions of years. In all of NASA’s and China’s plans for long-term settlement on the Moon, relatively few square miles at the south pole of the Moon matter the most.
New boss at ULA. United Launch Alliance has promoted Chief Operating Officer Mark Peller to president and CEO, succeeding Tory Bruno, who left ULA in December to develop and manage national security programs at Blue Origin, Aviation Week and Space Technology reports. Peller joined ULA at the company’s formation in 2006 and most recently led development of the Vulcan rocket, which successfully debuted in 2024 but has been grounded since early this year by a problem with its solid rocket boosters.
Taking the reins… Peller will have his work cut out for him. ULA, a 50-50 joint venture between Boeing and Lockheed Martin, lost its long-standing position as the Pentagon’s preferred launch contractor last year. That was before ULA grounded the Vulcan rocket following an anomaly with one of its strap-on solid-fueled boosters on a launch in February. The rocket overcame the malfunction and still delivered its payload to orbit, but it was the second time such an anomaly has occurred in the last three Vulcan missions. It’s not clear whether ULA will be able to resume Vulcan launches before the end of the year as engineers redesign parts of the booster’s nozzle structure. In the meantime, Boeing and Lockheed Martin last month confirmed they guaranteed a loan to ULA to help it through “financial challenges” caused by the grounding.
Next three launches
August 21: Falcon 9 | Starlink 10-39 | Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida | 15:14 UTC
August 22: Falcon 9 | Starlink 15-20 | Vandenberg Space Force Base, California | 07:25 UTC
August 24: Long March 5 | Chang’e 7 | Wenchang Space Launch Site, China | 00:05 UTC
Stephen Clark is a space reporter at Ars Technica, covering private space companies and the world’s space agencies. Stephen writes about the nexus of technology, science, policy, and business on and off the planet.
