articles.title: A third of web pages published since ChatGPT's launch show signs of AI authorship, study finds | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Over one-third of web pages published after the release of ChatGPT show signs of being written by AI, according to a new study from Pew Research released on Thursday. The report corroborates other studies that detail how much of the web’s newer web pages are now either written by or “substantially edited” by AI, the firm says.
It also arrives shortly after internet infrastructure provider Cloudflare reported that bot web traffic had overtaken human web traffic — a milestone that was reached sooner than the company had estimated.
Pew’s data, however, is focused not on who or what is browsing the web, but on what is being browsed. And apparently, much of it is bots reading web pages written by other bots.
To compile the report, Pew said it used the Common Crawl web archive to collect nearly half a million English-language web pages from the past five or so years, starting a couple of years before ChatGPT’s November 2022 release. Pew then used Open Pangram’s technology to detect how many were likely written or heavily edited by AI.
In a random sample of 10,000 web pages collected in July 2026, around 10% showed “significant signs of AI authorship,” Pew said.
However, Pew pointed out that a random sample like this would inevitably include older web pages — ones published before AI writing tools even existed, and therefore couldn’t have been AI written.
To get a better sense of how much of the web is now being written by AI, Pew filtered out the older web pages and focused only on those published after the release of ChatGPT.
In this same snapshot with the older pages removed, signs of AI authorship were found in over one-third (35%) of the pages.
Drilling down into domains themselves, Pew found that URLs with a .com domain showed signs of AI authorship at around 10x the rate of a .edu or .gov domain (both of which were around 1% AI authored). In addition, .org domains had only a 4.6% rate of AI authorship.
Of course, this analysis is not perfect. Pangram, like other AI-detection tools, can misclassify pages as AI written when they weren’t. But at scale, the data is likely at least directionally correct.
In addition, Pew found that other supposed tells of AI authorship had also increased over the years, like the use of em dashes, Oxford commas, and phrasing like “it’s not X, it’s Y,” among other things.

articles.title: A dumpling shop becomes a poster child of AI adoption in China
articles.text:
If you have an AI agent, you can tell it to build a website, make a slideshow, or get you a table at a popular dumpling shop in Beijing.
The dumpling shop, called Jinguyuan, has made headlines in China for creating a “skill” that allows users to check out the menu, seek recommendations, or join the queue by talking to their personal AI agents — tools that can automatically carry out tasks on a phone or laptop. Skills are files that teach AI agents specific workflows.
The shop owner, 41-year-old Li Bo, told me he built the AI skill in April, as he witnessed the growing popularity of agentic AI tools. Li began envisioning a world where everybody asks their AI assistant to plan daily work and life, including what to eat. Li wanted his dumpling shop to be part of that future.
“Science and technology are a primary productive force,” Li told me, quoting China’s late leader Deng Xiaoping, who unleashed the historic reforms in 1978 that led to the country’s economic miracle in the following decades. “You always need to surround yourself with the most advanced productive force.”
In many developed countries, AI is primarily associated with job losses, threats to creativity, and sprawling data centers invading rural communities. Outside of the tech industry, relying on AI sometimes evokes a sense of shame similar to cheating. In New York City, where I live, few small businesses advertise how much they use AI, even though on the streets, menus and posters everywhere have the telltale signs of AI-generated imagery and typography.
When I speak with people living in China, I find many are similarly worried about AI’s impact on the job market and the tech industry’s exploitative nature, but at the same time, everyone is eager to adopt AI, seeing it as an inevitable way forward.
Crash courses on large language models flourish online. Office workers rush to experiment with new AI tools to avoid falling behind in the competitive job market. When the agentic tool OpenClaw went viral, people queued up to have it installed on their laptops. A 2025 survey by public opinion firm Ipsos found that among the 30 countries surveyed, the Chinese population expressed the highest level of excitement about AI.
Li studied telecommunications engineering at the Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications. After graduating with a master’s degree in 2010, instead of becoming an engineer like many of his classmates, he worked at hostels, peddled homemade desserts, and eventually partnered with a dumpling chef to open Jinguyuan near his alma mater, serving students and tech workers.
AI reignited Li’s excitement for tech. Besides the AI skill, he also vibe-coded a website tracking the queue status at Jinguyuan’s two branches, mostly with Alibaba’s coding tool Qoder. In July, Li partnered with an AI cloud provider to give every customer a token coupon worth 10 yuan ($1.50) that could be put toward model subscriptions.
Li admits his AI skill brings more media attention than actual usage, but he is proud of becoming a role model for AI adoption. “Someone needs to start using it, even when it’s not that good,” Li said. “When steam engines just came out, people joked that they were not as good as horses. But in the end, cars won out.”

articles.title: On connaît enfin le prix de la nouvelle voiture électrique de BYD aux 1 000 kilomètres d’autonomie
articles.text:
Les constructeurs automobiles chinois sont bien décidés à mener une offensive forte sur le marché. Et BYD n’est pas le dernier, bien au contraire. La firme basée à Shenzhen n’a pas chômé au cours des dernières semaines, avec quasiment une nouveauté par semaine. Parmi elles, on peut notamment citer la nouvelle berline Da Han, aussi connue sous le nom de Great Han. Officiellement présentée le 21 août 2026 au salon de Chengdu, où BYD a ouvert les précommandes, elle nous donne de nouvelles informations à son sujet.
On connaît désormais son prix, annoncé sur le site officiel du constructeur. La voiture est ainsi affichée à partir de 249 900 yuans, ce qui donne environ 31 800 euros seulement. Un tarif qui sera cependant fortement revu à la hausse si elle finit par arriver en Europe. Et ce en raison des droits de douane, sauf si elle finit par être produite sur le continent un jour.
L’auto se décline en cinq teintes de carrosserie, et laisse le choix entre des jantes de 20 ou 21 pouces. Son style nous rappelle la Han EV, vendue en France un peu plus tôt. La berline mesure 5,26 mètres de long pour 2 mètres de large et 1,51 mètre de haut. Elle profite aussi d’un empattement généreux de 3,13 mètres.
Avec ses 5,26 mètres, la Da Han joue dans la cour des très grandes berlines : elle dépasse une Tesla Model S ou une Lucid Air et se rapproche d’une Mercedes Classe S à empattement long. De quoi situer les ambitions de BYD, qui place cette voiture au sommet de sa gamme Dynasty.
Elle en profite également pour montrer son intérieur, qui s’offre pas moins de trois écrans, dont la diagonale n’a pas été confirmée. L’un d’eux est spécifiquement destiné au passager à l’avant. Le volume du coffre arrière n’a pas encore été annoncé, mais celui à l’avant promet 150 litres.
Une autonomie démentielle
Déclinée en plusieurs versions, la BYD Da Han s’offre une motorisation affichant une puissance comprise entre 496 et 764 chevaux. Elle est disponible avec deux ou quatre roues motrices.
Mais surtout, la berline embarque la nouvelle batterie Blade 2.0 développée par le constructeur chinois, qui fait appel à la chimie LFP (lithium-fer-phosphate). Celle-ci affiche ici une capacité de 102,326 kWh et offre une autonomie comprise entre 880 et 1 008 kilomètres selon le cycle chinois CLTC. Ce qui donnerait environ 750 à 850 kilomètres une fois convertie au cycle européen WLTP.
BYD annonce une puissance de recharge de pointe de 1 500 kW, censée permettre de passer de 10 à 70 % en cinq minutes et d’atteindre 97 % en neuf minutes. Toujours sur les technologies maison, la Da Han a droit à la conduite assistée God’s Eye B développée par le constructeur chinois.
Par ailleurs, le site Car News China explique que la nouvelle Da Han sera aussi déclinée en une version hybride rechargeable, qui ajoute un moteur thermique turbo de 1,5 litre. La batterie affichera une capacité de 54,489 kWh, tandis que l’autonomie en mode 100 % électrique devrait atteindre les 470 kilomètres CLTC (environ 400 km WLTP).
Verra-t-on cette BYD Da Han en Europe ? Aucun mot pour le moment de la marque sur le sujet, mais elle pourrait avantageusement remplacer la Han vendue sur nos marchés, aujourd’hui totalement dépassée. En outre, une production dans l’usine de Hongrie (qui ouvrira ses portes en fin d’année) lui permettrait d’échapper aux surtaxes douanières.

articles.title: Ticket weiterverkaufen: Was erlaubt ist – und wann eine Abmahnung droht
articles.text:
Tickets im Netz weiterverkaufen: Warum das riskant und teuer werden kann
Das Konzert ist ausverkauft, die Karten liegen längst bereit – und dann kommt etwas dazwischen. Was bei einem gebrauchten Fahrrad oder Smartphone selbstverständlich wäre, scheint auch bei Eintrittskarten naheliegend: Ticket bei eBay, Kleinanzeigen oder einer Ticketbörse wie Viagogo einstellen, Käufer finden, Geld zurückbekommen. Doch ausgerechnet bei Eintrittskarten kann ein solcher Privatverkauf erstaunlich kompliziert und im schlimmsten Fall teuer werden.
Das gilt im Übrigen auch umgekehrt für Kund:innen, die im Vorverkauf des schnell ausverkauften Events keine Karte bekommen konnten und daher auf den Zweitmarkt zurückgreifen müssen. Auch hier kann – von gefälschten Karten bis ausbleibender Lieferung – vieles schief gehen.
Wie problematisch der Handel mit Tickets auch für Verkäufer:innen werden kann, zeigen aktuell unter anderem Abmahnungen rund um die Tour der Toten Hosen. Mehrere auf solche Fälle spezialisierte Kanzleien berichten von Schreiben an Ticketbesitzer, die Karten für die Tour 2026 über nicht autorisierte Plattformen angeboten haben sollen. Je nach Fall können dabei die Abgabe einer Unterlassungserklärung, Kosten oder Schadensersatzforderungen verlangt werden. Zusätzlichen Ärger kann das Verwenden von Logos oder offiziellen Veranstaltungsbildern verursachen.
Dabei geht es nicht zwangsläufig darum, dass jemand mit den Karten Gewinn machen wollte. Schon das öffentliche Angebot auf einer nicht zugelassenen Plattform kann nach den jeweiligen Ticketbedingungen problematisch sein. Ähnliche Fälle gab es ja in der Vergangenheit auch im Zusammenhand mit Fußballspitzenspielen, etwa beim DFB oder bei Bundesligavereinen.
Wann man ein gekauftes Ticket weiterverkaufen darf
Auch wenn das erst einmal überraschend klingt – schließlich hat man die Karte ja ordnungsgemäß erworben und bezahlt – ist es durchaus üblich, dass sich Tickets nicht wie alle anderen Waren verkaufen lassen. Das hat damit zu tun, dass die Plattformen verhindern wollen, dass Dritte damit handeln und sich das knappe Gut der Eintrittskarte gezielt zum Weiterverkauf sichern.
Denn generell gilt, dass einzelne nicht personalisierte Eintrittskarten in vielen Fällen verschenkt oder im privaten nichtgewerblichen Rahmen weiterverkauft werden dürfen, wie auch die Verbraucherzentrale bestätigt. Umgekehrt können der Veranstalter oder die Vermarktungsplattform festlegen, dass das Recht, die besagte Veranstaltung zu besuchen, an Bedingungen geknüpft sein kann.
Diese Allgemeinen Ticket-Geschäftsbedingungen, kurz ATGB, sollten Kund:innen im Vorfeld lesen. Diese können eben auch den Weiterverkauf untersagen oder festlegen, dass Tickets nicht zu einem höheren Preis als dem ursprünglichen verkauft werden dürfen. Übrigens kann also deshalb nicht nur der kommerzielle Weiterverkauf, sondern schon das öffentliche Angebot über nicht autorisierte Internetplattformen ausgeschlossen sein.
Üblich ist in vielen Fällen auch geworden, dass Tickets personengebunden sind und daher umgeschrieben werden müssen. Auch hier kann es Fristen, Beschränkungen oder sonstige Regeln geben – etwa, dass die Umschreibung an den Besitzerwechsel über eine bestimmte Plattform gebunden ist.
Allerdings hat sich der Bundesgerichtshof schon 2008 ausführlich mit Weiterverkaufsbeschränkungen bei Fußballtickets beschäftigt und bestätigt, dass vertragliche Beschränkungen des gewerblichen Weiterverkaufs durchaus Gültigkeit haben können. Hierbei ist aber der konkrete Vertrag, die einbezogenen Ticketbedingungen und die Art des Verkaufs – und ob der / die Erstkäufer:in von all dem Kenntnis hat.
Veranstalter wollen Zweitmarkt eindämmen – und haben gute Gründe
Auf die Fans wirken solche Regeln wie der Versuch, den eigenen Ticketshop gegen Konkurrenz abzuschotten, doch viele Veranstalter haben gute Gründe dafür: Zum einen kaufen professionelle Händler:innen bei besonders gefragten Konzerten oder Fußballspielen große Mengen der knappen Karten auf, um sie anschließend mit hohen Aufschlägen weiterzuverkaufen.
Auch mehrfach verkaufte oder gar nicht existente Tickets sorgen für Ärger und Stress. Bei Fußballspielen können Sicherheitsfragen hinzukommen, etwa wenn Tickets in bestimmten Fanbereichen an Anhänger der gegnerischen Mannschaft weitergegeben werden.
Dass der Zweitmarkt tatsächlich für erhebliche Probleme sorgt, bestreiten auch Verbraucherschützer:innen sowie der Bundesverband der Konzert- und Veranstaltungswirtschaft nicht. Letzterer forderte daher kürzlich sogar schärfere gesetzliche Regeln, vor allem im Hinblick auf fehlende Transparenz über Originalpreise sowie auf ungültige oder mehrfach verkaufte Eintrittskarten.
Auch Verkäufer gehen erhebliche Risiken ein
Während sich die privaten Verkäufer:innen schon vor dem Einstellen genau informieren sollten, ob und zu welchen Konditionen sie das überhaupt dürfen, liegen die Schwierigkeiten für Käufer:innen oft an anderen Punkten.
Ein großes Problem ist, dass der Einlass über den Barcode-Scan erfolgt – sodass es vorkommen kann, dass trotz gültigem Papierticket der Einlass verwehrt wird. Das ist dann der Fall, wenn etwa aufgrund eines Verkaufsbildes bereits jemand anders (meist auf digitalem Weg) eingecheckt hat. Aus diesem Grund sind in vielen Gruppen, in denen Tickets angeboten werden, jene mit gezeigtem Barcode „verbrannt“ und werden angesichts des Risikos nicht mehr gekauft.
Personalisierte Tickets ohne Umschreiben zu kaufen ist dabei eine besonders schlechte Idee, denn oftmals wird bei Einlass geprüft, ob der auf der Eintrittskarte eingetragene Name mit einem Ausweisdokument übereinstimmt. Wer eine solche Karte gebraucht erwirbt, riskiert also, trotz seines echten und bezahlten Tickets draußen auf dem Parkplatz zu bleiben.
Weitere Probleme können App- oder Mobile-Tickets machen, soweit diese an ein Benutzerkonto oder einen dynamischen QR-Code gebunden sind. So bietet etwa Ticketmaster Mobile-Tickets, deren Barcode sich alle 15 Sekunden verändert, sodass ein Screenshot beim Einlass nicht ausreicht. Eine offizielle Ticketübertragung generiert dagegen einen neuen QR-Code für den Empfänger.
Was bei Konzertabsagen noch wichtig ist
Wer also nur ein Bildschirmfoto oder eine PDF-Datei geschickt bekommt, riskiert nicht nur, dass das Ticket doppelt verkauft wurde, sondern könnte auch draußen bleiben. Dabei hilft der bei vielen Plattformen und Zahlungsdiensten übliche Käuferschutz nicht zwangsläufig. Kleinanzeigen schließt beispielsweise digitale Güter wie Tickets vom
eigenen Käuferschutz über „Sicher bezahlen“ aus.
Wer ein Ticket über den Zweitmarkt kauft, sollte daher nicht nur die Personalisierung und eine mögliche Umschreibung prüfen, sondern auch klären, ob die Weitergabe laut den Ticketbedingungen überhaupt erlaubt ist. Zu klären ist auch die Frage, ob im Rahmen eines privaten Geschäfts die Gewährleistungs- und Rückforderungsmöglichkeiten eingeschränkt sind – dann wird die Durchsetzung von Ansprüchen schwieriger. Denn oftmals können Erstattungen dann nur über den ursprünglichen Käufer abgewickelt werden. Bei Ticketmaster bleibt beispielsweise nach einer Ticketübertragung der ursprüngliche Käufer Ansprechpartner für Erstattungen und veranstaltungsbezogene Kommunikation.
Eine Eintrittskarte mag also aussehen wie ein einfaches Stück Papier oder ein QR-Code. Rechtlich und technisch steckt aber inzwischen deutlich mehr dahinter. Insofern kann der vermeintlich harmlose und sichere Verkauf eines Konzert- oder Fußballktickets deutlich riskanter sein als der Verkauf anderer Waren.

articles.title: Bring the Fire: Play Games on GeForce NOW With New Firefox Browser Support
articles.text:
It’s a new way into the cloud.
GeForce NOW welcomes Firefox support to the cloud, opening up another way to jump into high-performance PC gaming straight from the browser, starting today. Whether on a school laptop or everyday PC, it’s now even easier to play supported PC games without downloading a dedicated app.
Plus, discover 12 new games streaming from the GeForce NOW library this week, led by Gallipoli.
No Downloads. Just Firefox.
GeForce NOW is now supported on Firefox, expanding access across even more devices.
Members can outfox big downloads and jump into high-performance PC gaming directly from the browser — no waiting on lengthy game installs or updates. The experience delivers GeForce RTX-powered performance at up to 1440p and 120 frames per second for GeForce NOW Ultimate members.
Simply download the latest version of Firefox, head to play.geforcenow.com and start playing. The cloud handles the heavy lifting, so games are ready to play without taking up valuable storage space on the device. Firefox joins Chrome, Edge and Opera in supporting GeForce NOW on Windows browsers.
Deploy the Games
Land on the beaches of the Gallipoli Peninsula in BlackMill Games’ Gallipoli, the latest entry in the WW1 Game Series. Fight as soldiers of the British and Ottoman Empires in intense 25v25 objective-based battles across coastal shores, deserts and urban battlefields, with 10 historical classes and over 50 authentic weapons and equipment options.
Teamwork is key in its grounded, one-shot-one-kill combat. Take command as an Officer, provide cover as a Heavy Machine Gunner or Sniper, keep the squad going as a Stretcher Bearer and more while navigating challenging campaigns.
Head to the frontlines from the cloud with no lengthy game downloads or installs taking up local storage space. Play directly in the newly supported Firefox browser, or take the action across PCs, Macs, Chromebooks, handhelds and more with GeForce NOW cloud saves.
In addition, members can look for the following games streaming throughout the week:
- Stars Reach (New release on Steam, Aug. 18)
- The Sinking City 2 (New release on Steam, Aug. 18)
- Gallipoli (New release on Steam, Aug. 20)
- DIVE or DIE – Children of Rain (Steam)
- Escape the Backroom (Xbox, available on Game Pass)
- Hell Is Us (Xbox, available on Game Pass)
- High on Life (Steam)
- High on Life 2 (Steam and Xbox, available on Game Pass)
- Parcel Simulator (Steam)
- Starvester (Steam)
- The Thaumaturge (Xbox, available on Game Pass)
- Tomb Raider IV-VI Remastered (Epic Games Store)
Dates listed above reflect when games are released on their respective stores. GeForce NOW availability may vary, as games are onboarded after release and added throughout the week. Keep an eye on GeForce NOW channels and GFN Thursdays for availability updates on announced titles.
To try GeForce NOW in Firefox, start with a GeForce NOW day pass and experience premium cloud gaming directly from the browser. If members later upgrade to a Performance or Ultimate membership, the cost of the day pass can be applied toward the first membership purchase.
What are you planning to play this weekend? Let us know on X or in the comments below.

articles.title: Early Cerebras investor Adit Singh joins Mayfield as infrastructure partner | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Adit Singh was a partner at Foundation Capital when he helped source and co-lead the first funding round into then-obscure chip startup Cerebras.
By the time Cerebras held its blockbuster IPO in May, Foundation Capital held a roughly 7% stake, making it the third-largest shareholder in the company, which now trades at a valuation of nearly $50 billion.
Singh now has a new VC firm to call home: On Thursday, he said he’s now joined the 57-year-old Mayfield as an infrastructure partner.
At Mayfield, Singh will invest in hardware, infrastructure software, cybersecurity, and physical AI. He says it was the firm’s strength in semiconductors that drew him to the role.
“If you look at Mayfield’s semiconductor portfolio, it’s probably the best in the market right now,” Singh told TechCrunch, pointing to Mayfield’s investments in Upscale AI, which was recently valued at $2 billion, and Lumilens, which just raised $700 million at a $5.5 billion valuation.
“I’m a chip designer by training,” Singh said. “My secret sauce is being able to look at any workload and see how it works from the application all the way down to the transistor.”
He credits his background in electrical engineering to helping him recognize the potential in Cerebras 10 years ago. However, Singh didn’t stick around as an investor at Foundation. In 2017, he co-founded Neotribe Ventures, and after spending four years leading the firm, he joined early-stage firm Cota Capital.
Singh says he decided to join Mayfield in large part because the size of seed infrastructure deals has ballooned in recent years. While smaller funds often get priced out of mega-seed deals, Mayfield’s $3 billion in assets under management allows it to write seed checks of up to $20 million.
Mayfield managing partner Navin Chaddha told TechCrunch that despite knowing Singh for 15 years and sitting on three startup boards together — including Upscale AI and unicorn AI startup Velaura AI — it still took some time to convince him to join the firm.
“We have been talking for a long time, and this time stars aligned,” Chaddha said.

articles.title: “It’s laughable”: Global AI experts challenge Zuckerberg’s “AI for everyone”
articles.text:
On August 10, Mark Zuckerberg published a letter titled “The Future for Everyone,” a manifesto laying out his vision for how superintelligence could improve people’s lives, expand human capability, and distribute the benefits of artificial intelligence more broadly.
Zuckerberg advocated for wider distribution of AI access across countries and companies as “the path to a positive AI future,” sharing ways in which Meta is trying to make it happen.
Rest of World spoke to six AI observers from around the world about what they made of the letter, and whether AI can really become the great equalizer Zuckerberg envisions.
Some asked who gets to decide what “everyone” means. Others highlighted how access doesn’t always equal power.
Their responses have been edited for length and clarity.
“Grossly overstated economic benefits”
Chinasa T. Okolo, founder and scientific director of policy incubator Technecultura, and the inaugural policy lead of research organization Black in AI
AI infrastructure investments in African countries have yet to yield any significant tangible benefits. Kenya is pausing its Microsoft and G42-backed geothermal data center due to grid constraints, and forthcoming efforts like Cassava AI’s Nvidia-powered AI factories are likely to exacerbate grid stability concerns in countries like South Africa and Nigeria.
Meta has grossly overstated the economic benefits of its data centers, not only in this manifesto but also through extensive advertising campaigns focusing on smaller rural towns that traditionally hosted manufacturing or mining plants that have largely gone bust.
The labor benefits of data centers are primarily concentrated during construction, and once operational, they employ only a small fraction of permanent workers. While there is a marginally increased impact on home prices, this benefit doesn’t translate to local wages. Data centers are also associated with negative health and environmental impacts, which are likely to be even more challenging in African countries, which have fewer protections and lack the ability for governments to oversee strict compliance if environmental laws exist.
“Excludes people at the margins”
Sagar Vishnoi, director and co-founder of Future Shift Labs
Zuckerberg’s definition of “everyone” largely excludes people at the margins of the digital ecosystem: speakers of low-resource and tribal languages, shared-device households, communities with intermittent connectivity, and populations for whom digital infrastructure remains uneven.
If companies genuinely want AI to educate billions, investment cannot stop at bigger models. It has to extend to building open language infrastructure — consent-driven data sets, community-led language digitization, and compute access for local researchers and developers.
Trust will ultimately depend less on how much data AI can collect and more on whether platforms can demonstrate accountable enforcement, independent oversight, and protections that work across diverse legal and social contexts — not just within Silicon Valley’s institutional framework.
“Overlooking a fundamental reality”
Mark Mulobi, products and practices associate at global nonprofit Digital Impact Alliance
As a Kenyan, what resonates most with me in this vision is the potential for AI to act as a personal tutor — helping people learn, build skills, and access new opportunities. But the promise of “AI for everyone” risks overlooking a fundamental reality: Not everyone is online, digitally proficient, or able to engage with AI in English.
Realizing AI’s potential in Kenya — and across Africa — requires confronting the last-mile realities that still shape who can participate: reliable electricity, high-speed internet, affordable devices, and meaningful access in rural and underserved communities. It also requires deliberate investment in African languages and local knowledge systems. Without those investments, AI risks widening existing digital divides rather than becoming the empowering, inclusive technology that this vision aspires for it to be.
“A vector of U.S. power”
Juan Ortiz-Freuler, co-founder of global civil society coalition Non-Aligned Technologies Movement
Meta is so big it runs afoul of many different interest groups. These contradictions become more acute as the U.S. expects its private multinational tech corporations to play a key role in upholding U.S. hegemony, which often contradicts its profit-driven motives.
So while the first sections of the document target the global community — and regulators in places like Brazil, India, Turkey, and Nigeria — with a message of transparency, horizontality, and willingness to cooperate broadly, the latter sections are directed to U.S. regulators and power brokers who expect Meta to be a vector of U.S. power.
While Facebook is not a data-center company, it is an intelligence company. Its profit interest here comes not with increasing compute but with relying on humans to help untangle the relations between people and things. … Essentially, Facebook is redistributing tasks to its users across the world while training a central machine to understand the complex web of relations that underlie the world of symbols it was fed as text. It will use this to optimize its machines for a variety of tasks (curation, targeting), which it acknowledges it will also put at the service of the US government and the America First agenda.
“It’s laughable”
Abeba Birhane, founder of Trinity College Dublin’s AI Accountability Lab
Zuckerberg’s claim of “AI for everyone” is nothing new.
Decades ago, when Facebook overtook much of the African continent, Zuckerberg’s motto was something like, “connecting the rural and unconnected women across the continent.” Now, with a full grip on the continent’s digital infrastructure, Facebook/Meta has amassed populations’ data, monopolized the digital sphere, and controls the information ecosystem, with no observable benefit to the actual rural women it once boasted it would benefit.
Facebook has since exploited cheap or unpaid labour of data workers, extracted our resources, and caused enormous harm through disinformation, misinformation, and malinformation, while the corporation’s response when it is called out has been to displace accountability at any cost and gaslight the very people it claimed to help.
Looking beyond Africa, nobody should take Meta or Zuckerberg’s letter to “benefit everyone” seriously when the corporation that continues to silence criticism, retaliates against its own workers for exposing its technology’s harms, buries evidence of harm to minors, actively launches problematic products (the perv glasses) when overworked and underfunded civil society organizations have their attention focused elsewhere, and continually violates its legal obligations somehow claims to have people’s — especially vulnerable groups’ — best interests at heart. It’s laughable.
“Many aspects of trust that this letter omits”
Priya Vora, CEO of global nonprofit Digital Impact Alliance
Technology must be grounded in four guiding principles: participation, agency, choice, and trust. The letter speaks to participation, but meaningful participation requires people to have agency and choice — and to trust the systems they are being asked to use.
Governments can establish the rules of the road, but companies have to earn people’s trust through their actions. That means designing AI hand in hand with users — especially with those for whom accessibility needs are high — being transparent about how data and AI systems are used, and, crucially, giving people meaningful recourse when AI gets something wrong.
There are many aspects of trust that this letter omits. Trust is multidimensional, and those dimensions need to be considered from the outset and throughout the development and deployment of AI if we want these technologies to truly work for everyone.

articles.title: A New Approach to Open Source AI: A Framework for Openness | The Mozilla Blog
articles.text:
A New Framework for Open Source AI
Open or closed AI isn’t a fringe question anymore; it’s a live policy debate, with real consequences for who gets to build, audit, and compete in the AI ecosystem. But as that debate plays out in Washington, Brussels, and beyond, the harder questions are still very much up for discussion. What does meaningful openness actually require? Where should the guardrails sit? And who gets a say in setting them?
That’s exactly the gap a group of us set out to close two years ago.
Back in 2024, Mozilla and the Columbia Institute of Global Politics brought together more than 40 researchers, builders, and policy experts for the Columbia Convening on Openness and AI. The goal was simple to state, but hard to do: figure out what “open” actually means once you’re talking about foundational models rather than traditional software, and build a shared vocabulary that researchers, developers, policymakers, and civil society could all work from.
The convening was the start of a years-long effort to turn a room full of perspectives on openness into something durable and useful for developers, builders, and policymakers alike. Recently, that effort reached a new milestone: Communications of the ACM published “Unpacking Open Source AI: Toward a Framework for Openness in Foundation Models,” which I co-authored alongside a host of other allies spanning academia, industry, and civil society.
The paper outlines a framework that does something the open source AI debate badly needs. It stops treating “open” as a single switch you flip on or off. Instead, it breaks the AI stack down into its component parts – data, code, model weights, documentation, and more – and looks at how openness at each layer shapes who actually gets to inspect, use, and build on a system. That kind of specificity matters. A lot of the current policy debate treats open source AI as a monolith, when in reality the details of what gets shared (and how) are what determine whether openness delivers on its promise of safety, competition, and accountability.
A few of the framework’s ideas are worth pulling out. First, it treats openness as a gradient rather than a binary. A system can be open on weights while remaining closed on training data, or open on code while offering little documentation on how it was evaluated. The framework offers language to describe that mix precisely, instead of lumping it under one vague label. Second, it argues that safety can’t be assessed at the model level alone: what matters just as much is the surrounding system – the deployment environment, the safeguards, the moderation layers, and governance structures. That’s because a model’s real-world risk profile is shaped by all of it together, not by the weights in isolation. Critically, the framework deliberately stops short of prescribing one “correct” level of openness for every system. Instead, it gives developers, researchers, and regulators a common vocabulary to make and evaluate those tradeoffs on a case-by-case basis.
It’s worth pausing on who’s behind this work. Scroll through the author list, and you’ll find a genuine cross-section of the individuals and organizations contributing to moving the development of open systems forward. It’s a collection of people who’ve spent years arguing, in good faith and often across real disagreements, that open approaches can be a foundation for safer, more democratic, more accountable AI. That’s the same spirit that drove the original convening, and it’s what makes this paper a genuinely important milestone for our mission to make AI systems accessible to the many, rather than the few.
You can read the full paper here.
